title: SLA breach and priority ordering are observable on the case queue
risk: Breached cases are invisible in the queue, so customers with the oldest problems keep waiting while the dashboard reports a healthy service level.
preconditions: Tenant T1 with four cases at priorities P1..P4 and sla_due_at 2026-01-15T18:00:00Z in namespace cd-sla-*
Queue read at 2026-01-15T19:30:00Z, after two due times have passed

steps.action: Read the case queue ordered by priority and SLA due time
steps.expected: P1 cases precede P4 cases, and within a priority the earliest sla_due_at comes first

steps.action: Read the breach flags at the observation timestamp
steps.expected: CASE-T1-0011 is flagged breached with the elapsed overrun and CASE-T1-0012 is not flagged

steps.action: Attempt to assign priority P5 to a case
steps.expected: the assignment is refused and the priority vocabulary stays P1..P4

steps.action: Read the Resolution Time and First Response Time inputs for the breached case
steps.expected: both inputs are derived from the case timestamps and the breach is reflected rather than hidden

assertions: The queue ordering matches priority then earliest due time, with the breached P1 case first
Exactly one of the two cases is flagged breached at the observation timestamp
Resolution Time and First Response Time inputs reflect the case timestamps including the breach
forbidden: Hide a breached case from the operator queue
evidence: Queue listing with priority, sla_due_at and breach flag per case
KPI input rows for the breached case (first response and resolution timings)
cleanup: Delete the run-scoped cases for cd-sla-*; keep KPI inputs for the run window only
automation: Freeze the clock at a point after the due time so breach detection is deterministic; the oracle is the queue ordering and the breach flag, both read through the real projection.
